summary:
Taraba State stands under Nigeria's national criminal framework. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal in the territory since 1904 in the Northern Region and region-wide from 1916, and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA) now carries penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, applicable to all persons present in the country, visitors included.

The SSMPA reaches far beyond marriage. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation, participation in or support of gay clubs, societies and organisations, with prison terms of 10 to 14 years, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. The sources in this inventory do not document any Sharia application in Taraba itself.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised under the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in the national capital hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is routine. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice, reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in states that have adopted it. The same advisory records that the SSMPA criminalises attending, organising or promoting same-sex weddings and registering or publicly promoting gay groups.

Enforcement of the SSMPA has been arbitrary and punitive since inception. Human Rights Watch found that its passage was immediately followed by mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detention of LGBT people across the country, including the arrest without charge of 21 young men at a birthday gathering in Ibadan and repeated police detentions reported by interviewees elsewhere.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Taraba itself yields no statute, charge or incident in the available sources. The state's visitor assessment therefore rests on the national pattern: a nationwide SSMPA, documented arbitrary enforcement, and a documented risk of extralegal violence, with no Taraba-specific mitigation sourced.
tangentialFactors:
The 2026 UK advisory bundles legal exposure with administrative disruption, warning that mobile networks can be suspended and curfews imposed with little notice. Either measure would cut off messaging, location sharing and emergency contact at short notice.

Criminalisation in Nigeria has colonial statutory roots rather than recent legislative invention: the 1904 and 1916 prohibitions predate independence, and the SSMPA of 2014 reinforced them. Longevity of the regime means enforcement practice is entrenched rather than transitional.

The reporting that documents the worst outcomes is concentrated in Nigeria's largest urban centres and the national capital, which is a feature of source coverage as much as of incidence. Rural and mid-sized jurisdictions such as Taraba are under-reported, so an absence of named cases should not be read as an absence of risk.

Charge selection is visibly unrelated to the underlying conduct: the highest-profile trans person in the country was imprisoned on financial offences, while the formal anti-LGBT statutes supply leverage for extortion rather than for prosecution.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposed bans on public cross-dressing have been enacted is unresolved; the sources describe proposals and fear of them, not a statute in force.

No Taraba-specific statute, charge, arrest or incident appears in the inventory, and no source confirms whether Sharia penal provisions apply in Taraba. The finding that none is documented is an absence of sourcing, not a confirmation of non-application.

The status of the investigation into the August 2024 killing of Abuja Area Mama after February 2025 is unresolved; the last sourced position is that no suspects had been charged six months on.

The representativeness of the Wikipedia-derived national legal summary is unverified against primary Nigerian statute; it is used here only for framework dates and penalties that other sources corroborate.

Nothing in the inventory addresses gender-marker recognition on passports or identity documents, entry screening for trans travellers, healthcare access, or facility access, so those remain not sourced rather than favourable.
